children: Australian coal producer New Hope expects steady output at its Bengalla mine and a continued ramp up of operations at New Acland over the coming year, as the company positions itself to capitalize on a tightening coal market driven by ongoing conflict in the Middle East, its chief executive officer said.

New Hope reported a 63% drop in annual net profit on Tuesday as the Bengalla mine recovered from severe weather disruptions, but doubled its final dividend as output and sales exceeded guidance. Shares were 4.1% higher in early afternoon trading in Sydney.
"Really more of the same," CEO Rob Bishop said in an interview when asked what investors should expect from the year ahead.
New Hope plans to issue fiscal 2027 annual guidance alongside its first-quarter production report in November, as it has done in the past.

Investors will "see consistent production from Bengalla, so that should just be a continuation," Bishop said. New Hope has been consistently operating that mine, located in Australia's New South Wales state, at its target 13.4 million metric ton run-of-mine production rate in recent months, he said.
At the New Acland operation in neighboring Queensland state, New Hope is ramping production toward a target of roughly 5 million tons a year of saleable coal.

The site produced 3.3 million tons in fiscal 2026, a 17% increase year over year. "You'll see that move into the fours for FY27," said Bishop. "And, as a result, you'll see cost of production reduce at Acland as we get more tonnage to spread the fixed cost of that mine."

New Hope will likely keep a buy-back program in place to purchase shares when the it thinks there's value in doing so, said Bishop. Although, a rally in the miner's stock this year means it has to date only spent a fraction--about 10%--of its 100 million Australian dollar pot, equivalent to US$71.4 million.
"We'll take advantage of that when the share price is lower," he said.
Fanning its shares has been a rise in the price of coal New Hope sells for power generation.

Bishop said the coal market is tightening as oil and gas supplies are disrupted amid the conflict in the Middle East. Saudi Arabia's East-West Pipeline was shut after multiple drone attacks last week.
"Essentially that impacts the whole energy complex," Bishop said. "Security of supply is paramount."
Over the long term, New Hope is expecting coal demand to ratchet up due to electrification and data centers for the artificial intelligence boom, he said.
"I think even the most modest forecasts on energy demand are very strong, and it's not the case that any one form of energy supply is going to cover that off," said Bishop.

Beyond the Bengalla and New Acland mines, New Hope has a 26% stake in closely held Malabar Resources, which is ramping up the Maxwell underground mine in New South Wales. That mine will mostly produce coal for steelmaking.
New Hope has raised its stake in that company in recent years, including as recently as a year ago. Bishop said he "gets asked a lot" about New Hope's plans for that investment.
"It's an exciting asset," he said. "But we understand our ability to underground mine is emerging, and we feel as through the shareholders there and the operators there are doing a great job."
